Nevertheless, it seems to be the case that stress assignment in Aro is entirely predictable from a word’s syllable structure, albeit via a complicated set of rules. new_statements.quote: After each syllable has been assigned weight based on the rules specified in table 2.29, stress can then be assigned to a word according to the following set of rules: 1. The rightmost syllable with a weight of one is considered extrametrical (i.e. it is invisible to the rules governing stress assignment). 2. If there is only one remaining syllable that is not extrametrical, then stress is assigned to that syllable. 3. If the rightmost two syllables that are not extrametrical are of unequal weight, then stress is assigned to the heavier of these two syllables. 4. If the rightmost two syllables that are not extrametrical are of equal weight, then stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable (not counting any syllable that is extrametrical).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and predictable, assigned from the right edge within a two-syllable window: syllables get weight 1-4 (1 = open syllable with short /ə ɨ/; 2 = closed /ə ɨ/ syllable; 3 = /a i u/ nucleus or short-vowel+glide; 4 = long /e o ā æ/ or non-short vowel+glide); the rightmost weight-1 syllable is skipped as extrametrical; of the last two remaining syllables the heavier is stressed, and if they tie the penultimate one is stressed (default right-aligned trochee). Correlates: loudness and higher pitch, not duration.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress is described; only a single word stress is discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Author says stress 'seems to be' entirely predictable; affixation (mostly Cə- or C- prefixes, few unproductive suffixes) does not affect the rules; unstressed non-schwa vowels sporadically reduce to /ə/ in fast speech. /ə/ tends to repel stress. No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation/elicited word forms (illustrated with isolated words and inflected verb forms such as /key.ga.təy/); acoustic figures 2.16-2.17 from single words. Phrase-level intonation treated separately (ch. 11.1.1, rising intonation in polar questions). Language explicitly has no tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Drinfeld 2024 describes Aro proper (villages Selep, Brau, Mup, Fatundu, Wisamol, Afua, Riworip = Selep dialect; King, Kolembi = Meleng dialect), based mainly on the Selep dialect; he states the two Aro dialects barely differ phonologically. He treats Mukweym and Orok, which Glottolog's torr1259 'Aro-Mukweym-Orok' and ISO [tei] subsume, as separate languages NOT covered by the grammar (Glasgow & Loving 1964's 'West Torricelli' = Aro, 'East Torricelli' = Orok). So the stress statement applies to Aro, not necessarily to Mukweym or Orok.

sources.locator: Section 2.5.3 'Rules for assigning stress', p. 121 (PDF p. 144); also 2.5 intro p. 117 and Table 1.1 p. 10 ('Contrastive stress: no')
sources.note: Ch. 2.5 'Stress' (pp. 117-128): stress not contrastive, fully predictable from syllable structure via four syllable weights (vowel inherent length, glide, coda); rightmost weight-1 syllable is extrametrical; stress goes to the heavier of the last two non-extrametrical syllables, to the penultimate of them if equal weight; correlates are loudness and pitch, not length; prefixes (Cə) do not disturb the rules. Table 1.1 (p. 10): 'Contrastive stress: no'; no tone.
